amendments.rule: **An anarthrous substantive takes the English the ASV supplies to make it one.** A participle or adjective used as a noun with no article morpheme present still needs an English noun phrase, and the ASV supplies it: a bare *the*, or a pronoun with a relative — *him that*, *them that*, *they that*, *those that*. No article is present to take that English and nothing else licenses it, so it joins the substantive's own unit and is never `added`. `זֵדִים` → *the proud*, `צַדִּיק` → *the righteous*, `יִרְאֵי יְהוָה` → *them that feared Jehovah*, `עֹשְׁקֵי` → *those that oppress*, `עֹבֵד` → *him that serveth*. **Head on the word carrying the lexeme**, by rule 31's subtraction: *proud*, *righteous*, *feared*, *oppress*, *serveth*. This does not contradict rule 41's heading on the pronoun. There the supplied pronoun is the whole of what the article is rendered by, so it is the only candidate; here the substantive's own lexeme sits in the same unit and outranks a word the ASV supplied. Read whether an article morpheme is present, and let that decide which rule governs. Two riders. Where the Hebrew supplies a relative of its own, that relative takes the *that* and the supplied antecedent goes with it — `לַאֲשֶׁר לֹא עֲבָדוֹ` → *him that serveth him not* puts *him that* on `אֲשֶׁר` — since a present morpheme takes its English before a bare participle does. And where the ASV writes the antecedent once across coordinated substantives, the later ones take only what is written: `וְחֹשְׁבֵי שְׁמוֹ` → *and that thought upon his name* leaves the participle *that thought upon*, under rule 22. **A headless relative clause is read the same way, and its verb may be finite.** Where the Hebrew writes a relative clause with no antecedent noun and no `אֲשֶׁר`, the whole clause stands in a nominal slot and the ASV must supply a noun phrase for it: `אַחֲרֵי לֹא יוֹעִילוּ הָלָכוּ` → *walked after* ***things that do*** *not* ***profit***, `בְּלוֹא יוֹעִיל` → *for* ***that which doth*** *not* ***profit***. The supplied antecedent and relative join the clause's own unit and head on the word carrying the lexeme, exactly as *them that* joins a bare participle above and for the same reason: no article and no relative morpheme is present to take them, and nothing else licenses them, so neither is `added`. The unit is discontinuous around the negative or any other intervening word under rule 25, and a Hebrew noun the ASV recasts the same way — `מִבְטַחַיִךְ` → *those in whom thou trustest* — goes with it. **This governs only a clause with no antecedent of its own.** Where the Hebrew writes the antecedent and the ASV supplies a relative for a finite clause juxtaposed to it, nothing in this rule licenses that word: it subordinates a clause rather than making one a noun, and rules 30 and 55 are what decide it. **And a substantive the Hebrew writes is such an antecedent, whatever English this rule supplied to make it one.** An anarthrous participle or adjective for which the ASV has written *him that*, *they that* or *He who* is a written antecedent exactly as a common noun is, so a further relative the ASV writes over a finite clause juxtaposed to it answers to no morpheme and is `added` under rule 55: `נְאֻם שֹׁמֵעַ אִמְרֵי אֵל ... מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → *He saith who heareth the words of God ...* ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* leaves that *Who* `added`, while the same clause written with a relative of its own — `אֲשֶׁר מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` → ***Who*** *seeth the vision of the Almighty* — gives the word to the `אֲשֶׁר` under this rule's first rider. Do not read the supplied noun phrase as evidence that what follows is headless: ask whether a substantive stands before the clause, not whether that substantive's own English was written or supplied. Read what the ASV supplied, too, since the headless case writes an antecedent and a relative together — *things that*, *that which* — while a bare relative with no antecedent beside it subordinates a clause to what precedes and is rule 55's. Rule 41's articleless attributive is a third case again, and is decided there.
amendments.why: NUM.24.4 and NUM.24.16 are the same oracle, and the second drops the `אֲשֶׁר` the first writes before `מַחֲזֵה שַׁדַּי יֶחֱזֶה` while the ASV writes the same 'Who seeth' for both. The verse pass folded the supplied 'Who' into the finite verb under rule 46's headless-relative clause, reasoning that the clause stands in a nominal slot; but the antecedent is the participle `שֹׁמֵעַ`, which NUM.24.4 shows by attaching this very clause to it with a written relative. Rule 46's closing limit already sends that case to rule 55, and the same chapter had applied it correctly at NUM.24.6 ('As lign aloes which Jehovah hath planted', 'which' added). What the limit did not say is whether a substantive whose own English noun phrase this rule supplied counts as a written antecedent — the only reading on which the two verses could be treated differently. The amendment settles it where the limit stands, rather than leaving the over-broad headless sentence for whoever reads it first, and adds the test that actually separates the two constructions: the headless case supplies an antecedent and a relative together, a bare supplied relative subordinates.

conventions: A supplied English relative is placed by what stands before the clause it opens. Where a relative morpheme is written it takes the word (NUM.24.4, `אֲשֶׁר` → 'Who'); where the ASV recasts an articleless attributive as a relative clause the frame stays with the attributive under rule 41 (NUM.24.18, the italic 'who were' with `אֹיְבָיו`); and where the word merely subordinates a finite clause juxtaposed to a written antecedent it is `added` under rule 55 (NUM.24.6 'which' after `אֲהָלִים`, NUM.24.16 'Who' after `שֹׁמֵעַ`). A written substantive is such an antecedent even where this rule supplied its own English noun phrase, so the twin oracles NUM.24.4 and NUM.24.16 differ only in that one writes `אֲשֶׁר` and the other does not.

`עֲדֵי אֹבֵד` → 'shall come to destruction' takes the whole frame on `עַד` under rule 49's resultative clause, headed on 'to' (NUM.24.20, NUM.24.24). The italic 'shall come' of NUM.24.24's first clause is `added` under rule 20 instead, and the two are not in conflict: `מִיַּד כִּתִּים` keeps its own written 'from', so dropping the English leaves a lexical motion verb missing and no relation unstated, while dropping it before `עֲדֵי` leaves the terminative relation unsaid. Read whether the preposition already holds a word of its own before choosing.

`נְאֻם` heading an oracle is recast throughout this chapter as the finite 'saith', with its *nomen rectum* standing as the English subject of that verb and the unit discontinuous from it under rule 25 (NUM.24.3, 4, 15, 16, and the second `נְאֻם` of 3 and 15). The construct itself takes only 'saith'; no copula and no subject pronoun is placed with it.

report: Checked all 44 candidate lemma groups and read the dump end to end for added-vs-folded splits, which the keyed table cannot see. One real split: a supplied English relative standing before a juxtaposed finite clause. NUM.24.6 marks the 'which' of 'As lign aloes which Jehovah hath planted' added under rule 55, while NUM.24.16 folded the 'Who' of 'Who seeth the vision of the Almighty' into the finite verb under rule 46's headless-relative clause. Nothing in the source licenses the difference: both are asyndetic relatives standing after a written antecedent, and rule 46's own limit assigns that case to rules 30 and 55. NUM.24.16 is patched.

NUM.24.4 is deliberately left alone. There a written אֲשֶׁר stands before the same English 'Who seeth the vision of the Almighty' and takes it under rule 46's first rider; the presence of the relative morpheme is exactly the source difference that licenses the two verses reading differently, and after the patch the chapter's three supplied-relative cases divide on principle: written morpheme takes the word (v4), articleless attributive recast as a relative keeps it under rule 41 (v18, 'who were his enemies'), supplied subordinator over a juxtaposed finite clause is added (v6, v16).

The twin oracles otherwise agree unit for unit: NUM.24.3 and NUM.24.15 are word-for-word identical and were aligned identically, including the unrepresented suffix of בְּנוֹ and the 'whose' taken by the article of הָעָיִן; NUM.24.20 and NUM.24.21 both give the object marker the 'on' of 'looked on' under rule 16's first family, against the bare 'saw Israel' of NUM.24.2 where the ASV spends no word on the object relation. עֲדֵי אֹבֵד → 'shall come to destruction' is read the same way in NUM.24.20 and NUM.24.24.

NUM.24.24's two supplied verbs are decided in opposite directions and that is correct: the italic 'shall come' over the source-locative מִיַּד כִּתִּים is added, because מִן keeps its own written 'from' and subtraction removes a lexical motion verb rather than a relation, while 'shall come to' over the terminative עֲדֵי is rule 49's resultative frame. Recorded as a convention rather than left in one verse's notes. Supplied-word treatments are otherwise uniform: 'his' before 'eyes' is added in both v4 and v16; supplied object pronouns are added in v8 and v10 and aligned to a suffix wherever one stands (v9, v13, v17, v22); the infinitive absolute takes whatever word the ASV spends on the emphasis, 'altogether' in v10 and 'great' in v11.

None of the ten BSB disagreements is a genuine error; every one is a documented convention difference. The six unrepresented לְ are rule 27 (לֵאמֹר, v12), rule 40 (the ethical dative לְךָ of v11, the bare indirect object לִי of v13, לְדַרְכּוֹ of v25), rule 52 (the modal's bare complement 'cannot go beyond', v13) and rule 21 (the resultative הָיָה לְ of v22). The v12 הֲ is unrepresented because 'Spake I not' marks the question by inversion with no fronted auxiliary, which rule 17 states in terms; the v22 מָה is unrepresented because 'Until' carries nothing of the interrogative, so rule 30's one-word condition is unmet; the v14 paragogic he is tagged Sh and falls under rule 32; the two v14 articles are silenced by the demonstrative that takes the phrase's one determiner under rules 41 and 47; the v1 waw opens a bare apodosis and the first פַעַם of כְּפַעַם בְּפַעַם is the unrendered occurrence under rule 22. No accepted edge was changed to move the aggregate.
